episodes.summary_en: Hoya learns who wrote down the words of Joseon kings and why even the king could not read their notes. A real 1404 entry from the Annals shows how faithfully they recorded.
learning_goals: Know that 사관 (sagwan) were royal historians who recorded what the king and officials said and did.
Know that the historians' draft notes, 사초 (sacho), were supposed to be kept secret, even from the king.
Retell the 1404 entry in which King Taejong asked that the historian not be told of his fall, and the historian recorded it anyway.
Know that the Annals (실록, sillok) cover 472 years and 25 kings, from Taejo to Cheoljong.
Recognize and read 기록, 사관, 사초, 말 and 실록 with romanization.

scenes.narration_en: Hoya the little tiger has a big question: how do we know what kings said hundreds of years ago? Because people wrote it down! In the Joseon kingdom, special officials recorded the work of the royal court every day.
scenes.illustration: A small friendly tiger cub sitting on a stack of old thread-bound books, head tilted with curiosity; warm hanji-paper background.

scenes.narration_en: These officials were the 사관, the royal historians. Wherever the king met his officials, a historian was there, writing down what they saw and heard.
scenes.illustration: A Joseon palace hall: the king on a raised seat, officials kneeling in rows, and at the side a historian in official dress and a black hat writing with a brush on paper.

scenes.narration_en: Joseon had eight full-time historians, and many other officials also served as part-time historians. Their notes were called 사초, which means 'draft history.'
scenes.illustration: Close-up of hands holding a calligraphy brush over sheets of handwritten paper, an inkstone and ink stick beside them.

scenes.narration_en: The rule was strict: no one was supposed to read the 사초, not even the king. This helped the historians write fairly and protected them.
scenes.gloss_en: Even the king cannot see the sacho.
scenes.illustration: A closed wooden document box tied with a red cord; the king, seen from behind, walking past it without opening it.

scenes.narration_en: One day in 1404, King Taejong went hunting. His horse stumbled, and he fell off. Luckily, he was not hurt!
scenes.illustration: A gentle countryside scene: a brown horse that has stumbled on grass, and a king in plain riding clothes sitting up on the ground, unhurt, brushing off his sleeve.

scenes.narration_en: Taejong looked around and said, 'Do not let the historian know!' But that very sentence is in the Annals today. The historian wrote down even this!
scenes.gloss_en: Do not let the historian know.
scenes.illustration: The king glancing over his shoulder with a finger to his lips, while in the background a historian quietly writes; Hoya peeks from behind a tree, smiling.

scenes.narration_en: The historians' notes became the most important source for the 실록, the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty. The Annals cover 472 years and 25 kings, from Taejo to Cheoljong, and are on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.
scenes.gloss_en: the Annals (official history of each reign)
scenes.illustration: A long row of old thread-bound books standing in a wooden case, with Hoya proudly pointing at them.

episodes.notes: Taejong's fall is told exactly as the entry states (不傷, not hurt); the deer-shooting detail and season are omitted (lunar-to-solar conversion not verified from two sources). The secrecy rule is narrated as a rule ('supposed to'): the NIKH introduction notes that in practice some historians avoided frank writing out of fear and that leaks led to tragic purges (e.g., 1498), which are omitted as unsuitable for young learners. Revision: the English-language portal description quote ('Nobody was allowed to read the sacho...') was dropped from f4; the portal's Korean description sentence is kept in f5/f8/f9/f10 (re-checked against a saved copy of the portal page, 2026-10-09/10). The NIKH f9 quote was corrected to '일컫는다'. UNESCO Annals page is paraphrased, not quoted (unesco.org was unreachable on 2026-10-10 for re-quoting). Added 'from Taejo to Cheoljong' (the Annals do not include the Gojong/Sunjong reigns' records, so 25 kings, not 27). Alignment flag: BP05 1.A3 describes the Sillok as 'a diary people wrote every day' - inaccurate; the Sillok was compiled after each king's death from daily drafts (see story-sillok-mountain-archives). Designation numbers are deliberately not used. Narration scene 2: 'with brush and paper' removed (not stated in the cited sources).

episodes.title_en: The Annals Hide in the Mountains
episodes.summary_en: After a king died, officials turned the historians' notes into the Annals and guarded the books in archives far away in the mountains. Hoya follows the Annals from draft to mountain archive.
learning_goals: Understand that each king's Annals were compiled after his death by a temporary office, the 실록청 (Sillokcheong).
Know that used drafts were destroyed (in early Joseon, washed in a stream: 세초) to keep secrets and reuse paper.
Know that copies were kept in several archives (사고), many deep in the mountains, and that two scholars saved the Jeonju copy during a war.
Know that historians aired the books in the sun every few years (포쇄) and packed them with herbs.
Learn the words 사고, 산, 책, 햇볕 and 약초.

scenes.narration_en: When a king died, the next king's court set up a temporary office called the 실록청. Its officials collected the historians' 사초 and other court records to write the late king's Annals.
scenes.illustration: Officials in Joseon robes seated around low tables piled with papers and scrolls, sorting documents in a quiet hall.

scenes.narration_en: They wrote a first draft, corrected it in a second draft, and polished a final draft. Most of the Annals were then printed with movable type.
scenes.illustration: Three stacks of paper growing neater from left to right, then a wooden tray of small type blocks and freshly printed pages drying.

scenes.narration_en: And the used drafts? In early Joseon, they were soaked and washed in a stream near the government paper office. Secrets stayed safe, and the paper could be reused. This was called 세초.
scenes.illustration: A clear mountain stream with flat rocks; officials gently rinsing sheets of paper as the ink swirls away, Hoya watching from a rock.

scenes.narration_en: The finished Annals were kept in special archives called 사고. During a great war in the 1590s, the copies kept in Seoul, Chungju and Seongju were lost. Only the Jeonju copy survived.
scenes.illustration: A traditional archive building with a tiled roof and wooden walls; one lantern-lit doorway glowing, suggesting the one surviving copy.

scenes.narration_en: Two local scholars, An Ui and Son Hong-rok, used their own money to carry the Jeonju copy and other books to Naejangsan Mountain. They took turns guarding them until the books were handed to the government the next year.
scenes.illustration: Two scholars in plain traditional clothes and wide-brimmed hats leading a small ox cart loaded with wrapped book boxes along a misty mountain path.

scenes.narration_en: After the war, new copies were printed from the Jeonju copy, making five sets. Most went to archives deep in the mountains or on an island, such as Odaesan and Taebaeksan, where war was less likely to reach them.
scenes.illustration: A small walled archive compound nestled among pine-covered mountain ridges, clouds drifting below the peaks.

scenes.narration_en: The books were wrapped in oiled paper and red cloth, then packed in a wooden chest with herbs called cheongung and changpo, which helped protect them from bugs and rot.
scenes.illustration: An open wooden chest: books wrapped in red cloth, small cloth pouches of dried herbs tucked at the bottom and on top.

scenes.narration_en: Every few years, a historian traveled to each mountain archive on a clear day. The books were taken out and aired in the sun and breeze. This was called 포쇄. Hoya loves sunny days, too!
scenes.gloss_en: We dry the books in the sunshine.
scenes.illustration: Books laid open on mats in a sunny courtyard of a mountain archive, a historian checking pages while a breeze lifts them; Hoya basking nearby.

episodes.notes: Sources disagree on how many sets were newly printed in 1603-1606 (Korea Heritage Service and National Archives: four; Encyclopedia of Korean Culture: three printed plus the original and a proof copy); all agree on five sets in five archives, so narration says 'making five sets'. Poswae frequency also differs slightly (every 3 years in NIKH and the Annals entry; every 2-3 years in National Archives; the 진술축미 schedule of the Encyclopedia's poswae entry, i.e. every third year, though it often slipped), so narration says 'every few years'. Revision: 'red silk' changed to 'red cloth' (the poswae entry says 홍보 'red wrapping cloth'; only the National Archives says silk); the herbs' purpose is now stated generally ('protect from bugs and rot', per the poswae entry and the National Archives) rather than the National Archives' split into cheongung = insects and changpo = germs/fragrance; 'on a sunny day' replaced by 'on a clear day' (supported by two sources); the closing sentence 'Thanks to such care, the Annals survive today' was removed because it was not backed by a fact entry. Secho by washing is limited to early Joseon (later drafts were mostly burned). The Imjin War is mentioned only as 'a great war' with no violent detail. Omitted as out of scope or tragic: later moves to Jeongjoksan/Jeoksangsan, the Qing invasion, colonial-era removal of the Odaesan copy and its loss in the 1923 Kanto earthquake, the Korean War, and the 2006 return.

episodes.summary_en: At the Royal Secretariat, scribes wrote down the king's working day, every day, even the weather. Hoya learns why this giant diary is a treasure.
learning_goals: Know that the 승정원 (Seungjeongwon) was the king's secretariat that passed royal orders down and officials' opinions up.
Know that scribes called 주서 (juseo) wrote the 승정원일기, which survives for 1623-1910 in 3,243 books.
Know that each day's entry noted the weather, which researchers can use today.
Know that the original is in cursive 초서 (choseo), which was later rewritten in regular script, and that fires destroyed many volumes.
Use the patterns 날씨가 맑아요 and 일기를 다시 써요.

scenes.narration_en: Let's travel back in time with Hoya to the 승정원, the Royal Secretariat. This was the king's secretariat. It passed the king's orders down to officials and carried their opinions back up to the king.
scenes.illustration: Hoya stepping through a palace gate into a courtyard where officials carry folded documents to and from a hall.

scenes.narration_en: Six royal secretaries worked here, along with two scribes called 주서. The scribes wrote the office diary, the 승정원일기.
scenes.illustration: A row of six senior officials and two junior officials in formal court dress and black hats; the two junior ones hold brushes and paper.

scenes.narration_en: Each day, a scribe worked in front of the king together with a historian, jotting quick notes of the discussions. Later, a neat copy was made, and each month's diary was usually bound into one book.
scenes.illustration: A scribe and a historian kneeling side by side, writing fast while the king talks with ministers; in the corner, a finished thread-bound book.

scenes.narration_en: Every day's diary also noted the weather. Today, researchers can use these weather notes to study nature in the past.
scenes.illustration: A diary page drawn as simple brush lines beside a small sun symbol and a rain-cloud symbol; a modern researcher with a laptop comparing notes.

scenes.narration_en: The original diaries are written in a flowing cursive script called 초서, which is hard to read. In modern times, Korea's National Institute of Korean History rewrote them in clear, regular characters and published them.
scenes.illustration: Two sheets side by side: one with loose, swirling brush strokes, the other with tidy, upright brush strokes (no readable characters).

scenes.narration_en: Fires at the Royal Secretariat in 1744 and 1888 destroyed many diaries. Officials worked to rebuild them, partly using other records such as the court gazette.
scenes.illustration: Officials at desks surrounded by stacks of other records, carefully copying entries into new blank books; a calm scene with no flames.

scenes.narration_en: Today, 3,243 books survive, covering 1623 to 1910. The originals are kept at Seoul National University's Gyujanggak. The diaries are a National Treasure and, since 2001, part of UNESCO's Memory of the World.
scenes.illustration: Long wooden shelves filled with tall old books in a quiet modern archive, soft light, Hoya gazing up in wonder.

episodes.title_en: King Jeongjo's Diary of Daily Reflection
episodes.summary_en: As a young royal heir, Jeongjo kept a diary to look back on each day. It grew into the Ilseongnok, an official record of the court from 1760 to 1910.
learning_goals: Know that the 일성록 (Ilseongnok) began from Jeongjo's personal diary, kept when he was the royal grandson and heir (세손).
Know that Jeongjo was moved by Zengzi's words in the Analects about looking back on oneself every day, and kept a diary to reflect.
Know that from 1783 it became an official court record written by Gyujanggak officials, with headlines and details for easy reading.
Use 오늘, 반성, 일기를 써요 and 오늘을 돌아봐요.

scenes.narration_en: Hoya opens an old book about a young royal heir named Jeongjo. As the king's grandson and heir, he was called 세손. Even then, he kept a diary of what he said, did and studied.
scenes.illustration: A young royal heir in plain traditional clothes writing in a small book at a low desk by lamplight; Hoya reading a book about him in the foreground.

scenes.narration_en: Why? One reason was the words of Zengzi in the Analects about looking back on yourself every day. Jeongjo was deeply moved by them and wanted to look back on himself, too.
scenes.illustration: The prince pausing with brush raised, looking thoughtfully out of a window at an evening sky.

scenes.narration_en: His diary was called the Jonhyeongak Diary. After Jeongjo became king, he kept writing it himself. Hoya tries it too and asks, 'What did I do today?'
scenes.illustration: Split scene: King Jeongjo in royal dress writing at night; Hoya in his den with a tiny notebook, scratching his head.

scenes.narration_en: As state business grew, Jeongjo had too much to write himself. So in 1783, officials of the royal library, Gyujanggak, began writing the diary about state affairs, and the king approved it. His personal diary became an official record.
scenes.illustration: Scholars at the Gyujanggak library writing at desks, then presenting a bound book to the king, who reads it carefully.

scenes.narration_en: Its title, 일성록, is often translated 'Records of Daily Reflections.' Each entry starts with a short headline, and the details follow, which made it easy to read.
scenes.illustration: An open book page drawn with one bold line of strokes at top and smaller lines below (no readable text), a finger tracing the bold line.

scenes.narration_en: The 일성록 looks like a diary written from the king's point of view, but it was really an official government record. Today, 2,329 books covering 1760 to 1910 are kept at Seoul National University's Gyujanggak.
scenes.illustration: A modern library stack with rows of old thread-bound books in protective cases, a curator in gloves checking one.

scenes.narration_en: The 일성록 is a National Treasure, and in 2011 UNESCO added it to the Memory of the World. Hoya decides to write one line tonight: what went well today, and what to do better.
scenes.illustration: Hoya at night writing in a notebook by a small lamp, a crescent moon in the window, smiling.

episodes.notes: The Analects line: the Korean portal and Encyclopedia texts say '세 가지 기준' ('three standards'), Legge translates Analects 1.4 as 'on three points', and the Encyclopedia also glosses 日三省吾身 as 'three times a day'; because translations differ, the number is DROPPED from narration and the claim, and the Korean quotes in the sources are kept as printed. 'Why?' now says 'One reason': the Encyclopedia also records other readings (the word 省 may echo Yeongjo's 어제자성편; a political motive is also suggested). Naming: 한국민족문화대백과사전 says the final decision on the title cannot be confirmed (in 1781 others proposed 일성록 or 월계록, and Jeongjo objected only to the combined 일월통편), so 'Jeongjo named it' was REMOVED; the story says only that the title is 일성록 and UNESCO translates it as 'Records of Daily Reflections'. The 1783 transition and 'state business grew' are supported by the portal's Korean description and by the Encyclopedia (quoting Jeongjo's 군서표기 in the 홍재전서). The post-accession diary claim (f3) is supported by the portal and by the Encyclopedia ('정조의 일기는 즉위 후에도 계속되었는데'). The Chinese- and Japanese-language machine-translated portal descriptions were removed as sources (f6, f7). 'Every five days' and the 1776 accession year appear only in the portal text and are not in narration. UNESCO page wording is paraphrased (unesco.org unreachable for re-quoting). Framing 'Hoya opens an old book' keeps the story from presenting an imagined meeting with Jeongjo as fact. Omitted: 21 months of missing records; Jeongjo's father's story (tragic).

episodes.title_en: A Picture Record of a Royal Birthday
episodes.summary_en: Uigwe were detailed reports, full of pictures, of royal ceremonies and projects. Hoya opens the Wonhaeng Eulmyo Jeongni Uigwe, the record of King Jeongjo's 1795 celebration for his mother's 60th birthday.
learning_goals: Know that an 의궤 (uigwe) recorded a royal ceremony or project in words and pictures so later generations could follow it.
Know that uigwe list the people who took part, including craftspeople.
Describe a 반차도 (banchado): a long picture of a procession, usually drawn as if seen from above.
Know that the 1795 feast for Lady Hyegyeong at Bongsudang is recorded in the Annals and in the Wonhaeng Eulmyo Jeongni Uigwe, which was printed with metal type.
Learn 잔치, 그림, 어머니, 환갑 and 장인.

scenes.narration_en: When the Joseon court held a big event, such as a royal wedding, a banquet or the rebuilding of a palace, officials made an 의궤: a detailed report in words and pictures.
scenes.gloss_en: illustrated record of a royal event
scenes.illustration: An open old book with a colorful painted page of a ceremony beside a page of neat brush writing (no readable text); Hoya leaning in to look.

scenes.narration_en: Why? So that next time, people could hold the same kind of event properly. Each uigwe recorded the steps, the people, the costs and the materials, like a final report.
scenes.illustration: Officials checking items off against an open uigwe: bolts of cloth, bowls, flags and lanterns laid out in a courtyard.

scenes.narration_en: Uigwe even listed the people who took part, from high officials to skilled craftspeople. Their names and roles were written down, too.
scenes.illustration: A carpenter, a painter and an embroiderer at work in a palace workshop, each proud of their craft.

scenes.narration_en: In 1795, King Jeongjo traveled with his mother, Lady Hyegyeong, to the new city of Hwaseong in Suwon for a grand celebration of her 60th birthday.
scenes.illustration: A long, colorful royal procession winding along a road toward a fortress city; two ornate palanquins at the center.

scenes.narration_en: By the old lunar calendar, 1795 had an extra 'leap' month after the second month. On its 13th day, the king gave a grand feast for his mother at Bongsudang Hall in the Hwaseong temporary palace. The Annals record that day.
scenes.illustration: A festive palace hall with tables of food, musicians and dancers in bright costumes, and an honored elderly lady seated under a canopy.

scenes.narration_en: The king also gave gifts of silk to elderly people who took part in the celebration.
scenes.illustration: Smiling elderly men in plain traditional clothes receiving folded bolts of silk in a sunny courtyard.

scenes.narration_en: The record of this trip, the 원행을묘정리의궤 (Wonhaeng Eulmyo Jeongni Uigwe), is full of pictures. Some are 반차도: long pictures of a royal procession, usually drawn as if seen from high above, showing where everyone walked or stood.
scenes.illustration: A bird's-eye view of a long procession: rows of tiny figures, horses, flags and palanquins arranged neatly along a path.

scenes.narration_en: Unusually, this uigwe was printed with metal movable type, so more copies could be shared. Its pictures are prints, too. In 2007, UNESCO added the Joseon uigwe to the Memory of the World.
scenes.illustration: Small metal type pieces in a tray next to a freshly printed picture page and the printing tools beside it.

facts.claim_en: Uigwe record, in text and illustrations, major royal ceremonies and state projects such as royal weddings, banquets, funerals, receptions of envoys and the rebuilding of palaces.

episodes.notes: Narration omits the ages in the silk-gift entry (70+ and those turning 61) because they come from a single source; the Korean line '어르신' is a vocabulary item. 회갑 (source term) and 환갑 (everyday term) both mean the 60th birthday; 환갑 is taught. The feast date is given on the lunar calendar as recorded; the KHS English page says 'February 1795', which refers to the lunar leap 2nd month. The leap-month wording was rewritten simply ('an extra leap month after the second month'). The Hwaseong feast (13th of the leap 2nd month) took place during the 1795 trip celebrating her 60th year; her actual birthday fell in the 6th lunar month and the Encyclopedia notes a formal feast on 6/18 in Seoul, so narration says 'a celebration of her 60th birthday' and never says the Hwaseong feast was on the birthday itself. Revision: the uigwe is now named (원행을묘정리의궤); banchado described as 'long pictures' not paintings; 'woodblock' was REMOVED - Korean authorities (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture) say only 판화 (prints), and no Korean institutional source found says woodblock specifically (a Cambridge/Amsterdam UP page suggested by a checker did not mention woodcuts when re-fetched). The encyclopedia calls this 'the first uigwe printed with movable type'; narration says 'unusually' to stay conservative. UNESCO page text is paraphrased (unesco.org unreachable for re-quoting); UNESCO nomination-form quotes were re-checked against a saved copy of the PDF; the draft's banchado caption quote ('Banchado in color ... excellent clarity') could not be found in the PDF text and was replaced by the §1 Summary sentence on Banchado and Doseol. Omitted: the length of a painting (15.4 m, single source), page counts beyond f7, the story of Prince Sado (tragic), and the 1866 removal of Oegyujanggak uigwe to France and their 2011 return (war-related). PASS 3: second source for 판화 found (정병모, 판화사적 연구: 'prints' - and specifically 목판화, woodblock prints, with 정리자 metal type); narration stays at the more general 'prints'. Silk gifts (f6) confirmed directly in the original Annals entry text (命進饌時參班老人, 七十以上及六十一歲人, 各賜帛一匹); single primary source kept, no numbers in narration.

episodes.summary_en: How do Joseon records help people today? Hoya sees a fortress repaired from uigwe drawings, a festival that recreates a royal procession, scientists reading old weather notes, and the Annals open to everyone online.
learning_goals: Give at least two ways people use Joseon records today (restoring Hwaseong, recreating a procession, studying past weather, reading the Annals online).
Know that the Annals, Seungjeongwon Ilgi, Uigwe and Ilseongnok are all on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.
Say 기록은 보물이에요 and recognize 화성, 성, 행렬 and 날씨.

scenes.narration_en: Hoya has one more question: what do these old records do for us today? Let's visit some places where Joseon records are still at work.
scenes.illustration: Hoya with a small backpack standing at a crossroads with signposts shaped like a book, a fortress and a cloud (no text).

scenes.narration_en: Suwon Hwaseong fortress was finished in 1796. Every step of the building work was recorded in the Hwaseong Seongyeok Uigwe, with drawings of buildings and machines, and the sizes and amounts of materials.
scenes.illustration: A stone-and-brick fortress wall with a gate tower; beside it, an open book showing a drawing of a lifting machine with pulleys.

scenes.narration_en: Later, parts of the fortress were damaged. Workers followed the uigwe to restore it to its original shape, and repairs still rely on this record today.
scenes.illustration: Modern workers in helmets fitting stones into a fortress wall while one checks a page of old drawings on a tablet.

scenes.narration_en: Today, Suwon's Hwaseong Cultural Festival, the 수원화성문화제, includes a recreation of King Jeongjo's grand royal procession, based on the uigwe of his trip.
scenes.illustration: A modern street festival: people in colorful Joseon costumes marching with flags and a palanquin, families watching and waving.

scenes.narration_en: Scientists can study the weather notes in the Seungjeongwon Ilgi, written day after day for nearly 300 years, to learn about nature in the past.
scenes.illustration: A scientist at a computer showing a simple line chart, with an old diary open on the desk and a window showing rain clouds.

scenes.narration_en: The Annals were written in classical Chinese, which is hard for most people today. Translators turned them into modern Korean, and now anyone can read the translation online, along with the original text.
scenes.illustration: A child and a grandparent looking at a tablet showing two columns of text shapes, one old style and one modern (no readable characters).

scenes.narration_en: All four records you met, the Annals, the Seungjeongwon Ilgi, the uigwe and the Ilseongnok, are on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.
scenes.illustration: Four old books standing side by side on a shelf with a soft glow, each a different cover color.

scenes.narration_en: Hoya smiles. Thanks to people who wrote carefully long ago, we can still learn from the past. 'Records are treasures!' What will you write down today?
scenes.illustration: Hoya holding up a small notebook and brush, grinning, with the fortress, books and a sunny sky behind him.
